title: A Record Is an Argument
bigQuestion: When is a sports record fair to compare with another, and what evidence should change our minds about one?

story.title: 190 or 191?
story.kicker: Two baseball books on one library table give two different numbers for the same season.
paragraphs: A high school student named Maya is working on a history project at a Chicago public library. She has two baseball reference books open side by side. One was printed in the 1980s. The other is much newer. Both describe the 1930 season of Hack Wilson, a Chicago Cubs outfielder.

In 1930, Wilson had one of the greatest hitting seasons in baseball history. He hit 56 home runs, a National League record that lasted until 1998. He also drove in more runs than any player ever had in one season. A run batted in, or RBI, is a run that scores because of what a batter did.

The older book says Wilson had 190 runs batted in. The newer book says 191. Maya checks the years, the team and the spelling. Everything else matches. Only that one number is different. That one number matters, because Wilson's total is still the single-season major league record.

A librarian helps her find the answer. In 1999, Major League Baseball changed Wilson's total to 191. Researchers had studied old game accounts and found that one run from a 1930 game had been credited to a teammate instead of Wilson. Books printed before 1999 still show the old number.

Maya writes in her notes that a record is not carved in stone. People count it, write it down and check it again. Sometimes they find a mistake decades later. The record is only as strong as the evidence behind it.
story.think: Why might an official record change almost seventy years after the season it describes?

lessons.title: Keepers of the Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Records exist because governing bodies, official scorers and researchers decide what counts and write it down.
reading: In baseball, an *official scorer* decides many numbers during a game. The scorer rules whether a batted ball was a hit or an error, and whether a runner's run counts as an RBI. The Official Baseball Rules include a whole section on the scorer's job. A single decision in the press box can change a player's season average.

In track and field, records must be approved, or *ratified*, by a governing body. The International Amateur Athletic Federation was founded in Stockholm in 1912. It was renamed World Athletics in 2019. Before a world record is ratified, officials check the timing equipment, the wind reading, the measurement and a drug test taken after the event.

Private groups keep numbers too. The Elias Sports Bureau, founded in New York in 1913, became a longtime official statistician for Major League Baseball. In 1971, a small group met in Cooperstown, New York, and founded the Society for American Baseball Research, or SABR. Its members dig through old newspapers and box scores. Their research has corrected many records, including Hack Wilson's.

words.d: the person who decides hits, errors and other game numbers for the record
officially approved by a governing body after checking the evidence
the governing body for track and field, founded in 1912 and renamed in 2019
the Society for American Baseball Research, founded in 1971

look.title: One Call in the Press Box
look.text: A batter hits a hard ground ball. The fielder gets a glove on it but cannot make the play. In the press box, the official scorer must decide. If it is a hit, the batter's average goes up. If it is an error, the batter's average goes down and the fielder's record gets a mark.
look.prompt: Why does a record depend on a person's judgment and not only on what happened on the field?

check.q: What does ratified mean?
choices: officially approved after checking the evidence
check.why: A ratified record has been checked and approved by a governing body such as World Athletics.

check.q: When was the body now called World Athletics founded?
check.why: It was founded in Stockholm in 1912 and renamed World Athletics in 2019.

check.q: What does SABR do?
check.why: The Society for American Baseball Research, founded in 1971, studies old records and has corrected many.

lessons.title: One Season, Two Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Careful research can change an old record, so different record books can list different numbers for the same player.
reading: Hack Wilson's 1930 total of runs batted in was listed as 190 for almost seventy years. In 1999, Major League Baseball accepted research showing that one RBI from a 1930 game had gone to a teammate by mistake. The official total became 191. It is still the major league record for one season.

Ty Cobb's career hit total shows a different result. Cobb played from 1905 to 1928, mostly for the Detroit Tigers. For decades his total was listed as 4,191 hits. Researchers later found that one 1910 game appeared to have been counted twice. Some record books now list 4,189 hits, while others still list 4,191.

These cases show how an *official record* differs from a *revision*. An official record is the number a governing body accepts. A revision is a change made after new evidence is found. When Pete Rose passed Cobb in 1985, newspapers reported the moment against the 4,191 total. The dispute over two hits did not change who held the career record, but it shows that records are built from papers people can check.

words.d: the number or mark a governing body accepts as correct
a change made to a record after new evidence is found
a run that scores because of what a batter did; also called an RBI

look.title: Two Books, One Career
look.text: Book A, printed in 1975, says Ty Cobb had 4,191 hits. Book B, printed much later, says 4,189. Book B has a footnote: one 1910 game appears twice in the old daily records. Book A has no footnote. Both books agree on every other number about Cobb.
look.prompt: Which book gives you more reason to trust its number, and why?

check.q: Why did Hack Wilson's RBI total change in 1999?
choices: He was found to have used a corked bat.
Research found one RBI had been credited to a teammate.
The Cubs asked for a new total.
check.why: Research into 1930 game accounts found a run credited to a teammate, so the total went from 190 to 191.

check.q: What is a revision of a record?
choices: a change made after new evidence is found
a rule change on the field
a copy of an old box score
check.why: A revision changes a record because new evidence shows the old number was wrong.

check.q: Why do some books list 4,189 hits for Ty Cobb?
choices: He lost two hits to a rule change.
One 1910 game appears to have been counted twice.
check.why: Researchers found an apparent double-counted 1910 game, which would remove two hits.

lessons.title: The Asterisk That Wasn't
lessons.mainIdea: In 1961, a longer schedule made people argue whether Roger Maris's 61 home runs could be compared with Babe Ruth's 60.
reading: In 1927, Babe Ruth of the New York Yankees hit 60 home runs. The American League schedule then had 154 games. In 1961, the league added two teams and stretched the schedule to 162 games. That summer, two Yankees, Roger Maris and Mickey Mantle, chased Ruth's record.

On July 17, 1961, Commissioner Ford Frick announced a ruling. If a player passed 60 home runs within 154 games, it would be a new record. If he did it later in the season, the record books would need some mark to show the difference. Maris had 59 home runs after 154 games. He hit his 61st on October 1, 1961, the last day of the season, at Yankee Stadium.

People began saying Maris's record had an *asterisk*, a small star used in print to point to a note. No official record book actually put a star next to his name. The two marks were simply listed separately for years. In 1991, a committee on statistical accuracy under Commissioner Fay Vincent ruled that Maris alone held the single-season record. The argument was about *context*: the conditions around a record that affect how it is judged.

words.d: a small star printed next to something to point to a note
the conditions around an event that help explain it
the list of games a team plays in a season

look.title: Ford Frick's Ruling, 1961
look.text: A player who hits more than 60 home runs within his club's first 154 games will be recognized as setting a new record. If he does so only after 154 games, the record books should show a distinctive mark that it was done in a longer season.
look.cite: Ford Frick, Commissioner of Baseball, ruling announced July 17, 1961
look.prompt: What condition did Frick say made the two seasons hard to compare?

check.q: Why did Frick say Maris's record might need a mark?
choices: Maris used a new kind of bat.
The games were played at high altitude.
The 1961 season had 162 games instead of 154.
Maris played for a different league.
check.why: The schedule grew from 154 to 162 games in 1961, so Frick said a later record should be shown differently.

check.q: Did an official record book put an asterisk next to Maris's name?
choices: No; the records were listed separately, and the asterisk became a popular phrase.
Yes, and it is still there.
check.why: No official book used a star; people used the word for the separate listing until 1991.

check.q: What happened in 1991?
choices: A committee ruled that Maris alone held the single-season record.
check.why: A committee under Commissioner Fay Vincent recognized Maris as the sole record holder in 1991.

lessons.title: A Javelin Redesigned
lessons.mainIdea: When equipment changes, record keepers sometimes start a new list, as track and field did with the javelin in 1986.
reading: On July 20, 1984, Uwe Hohn of East Germany threw the men's *javelin* 104.80 meters in East Berlin. A javelin is a spear thrown for distance. His throw went so far that officials worried about the safety of people inside the stadium. Many throws were also landing flat, which made them hard to measure fairly.

The governing body answered with a new design. From 1986, the men's javelin had its center of gravity moved forward. The new javelin came down sooner and landed point first more often. Because the tool was different, record keepers started a new world record list. Hohn's mark stays in the books as the record for the old design.

Women's javelins were redesigned in the same way in 1999. Other sports show similar *equipment* changes. In the pole vault, athletes used bamboo poles into the 1940s, then metal poles, then fiberglass poles by the early 1960s. Heights rose quickly after each change. Each time, people asked whether new marks and old marks measured the same thing.

words.d: a spear thrown for distance in track and field
the tools and gear used in a sport, such as poles, balls and suits
the point where an object's weight is balanced

look.title: Two Javelins, Two Lists
look.text: World Athletics keeps two men's javelin marks in its history. Uwe Hohn threw 104.80 meters in 1984 with the old design. Jan Železný of the Czech Republic threw 98.48 meters in 1996 with the new design. The newer mark is shorter, yet it is the current world record.
look.prompt: Why would it be unfair to say Hohn's throw beats Železný's record?

check.q: Why was the men's javelin redesigned in 1986?
choices: to make it lighter for young athletes
because throws were going dangerously far and landing flat
check.why: Hohn's 104.80-meter throw raised safety worries, and flat landings were hard to measure.

check.q: What happened to the record list after the javelin was redesigned?
choices: A new world record list began.
Hohn's record was moved to the new list.
The event was dropped from the Olympics.
check.why: Because the tool changed, record keepers started a new list for the new design.

check.q: Which pole material came last in pole vault history?
check.why: Vaulters used bamboo, then metal, then fiberglass poles by the early 1960s.

lessons.title: Suits in the Pool
lessons.mainIdea: Full-body racing suits in 2008 and 2009 led to a burst of swimming records, and the governing body banned them from 2010.
reading: In 2008, swimsuit companies began selling new full-body racing suits. Some used panels of polyurethane, a smooth plastic material, instead of woven fabric. These suits helped swimmers float higher and move through water with less drag. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, many world records fell.

Even more records fell at the 2009 World Championships in Rome, where dozens of world records were set. Coaches and athletes argued about whether the times showed the swimmers or the suits. Some called the problem *technological doping*, meaning an unfair edge from equipment rather than from training.

FINA, the world governing body for swimming, changed its rules. From January 1, 2010, racing suits had to be made of *textile*, or woven fabric. Men's suits could reach only from the waist to the knee, and women's from the shoulders to the knee. Many records from 2009 stood for years after the ban. In 2022, FINA was renamed World Aquatics.

words.d: woven or knitted fabric
a phrase for gaining an unfair advantage through equipment
the world governing body for swimming, renamed World Aquatics in 2022

look.title: Two Swimmers, Two Suits
look.text: Swimmer A set a world record in 2009 wearing a full-body polyurethane suit. Swimmer B swims the same event in 2015 in a legal textile suit that reaches only to the knee. Swimmer B finishes a little slower than Swimmer A's record time.
look.prompt: Can you tell from the times alone which swimmer was faster? What else would you need to know?

check.q: What rule took effect on January 1, 2010?
choices: Racing suits had to be textile and limited in coverage.
Swimmers had to wear full-body suits.
Pools had to be made longer.
check.why: FINA required textile suits with limits on how much of the body they cover.

check.q: What does technological doping mean?
choices: using medicine to heal an injury
an unfair edge from equipment rather than training
breaking a record at high altitude
check.why: The phrase describes an advantage that comes from gear, as critics said of the 2008 and 2009 suits.

check.q: Where were dozens of world records set in 2009?
check.why: Dozens of world records fell at the 2009 World Championships in Rome.

lessons.title: Thin Air in Mexico City
lessons.mainIdea: Thin air at high altitude helps sprints and jumps, so records set there, like Bob Beamon's 1968 long jump, carry an extra argument.
reading: The 1968 Summer Olympics were held in Mexico City, about 2,240 meters, or 7,350 feet, above sea level. At that *altitude*, the air is thinner. Thin air pushes back less on a sprinter or jumper. It also holds less oxygen, which makes long races harder. Distance runners from high-altitude countries such as Kenya and Ethiopia did well in several long races there.

On October 18, 1968, Bob Beamon of the United States long-jumped 8.90 meters. The old world record was 8.35 meters, so he beat it by 55 centimeters. His mark lasted until 1991, when Mike Powell jumped 8.95 meters in Tokyo, near sea level. Four days earlier in Mexico City, Jim Hines had run the 100 meters in 9.95 seconds, the first electronically timed run under ten seconds.

Rules now handle some conditions but not others. World Athletics will not ratify a sprint or horizontal jump record if the *tailwind*, wind at the athlete's back, is above 2.0 meters per second. Altitude does not block a record, but results lists often mark high-altitude marks with an "A." Baseball faced a similar problem in Denver, about a mile high. In 2002, the Colorado Rockies began storing baseballs in a humidity-controlled room called a humidor.

words.d: height above sea level
wind blowing from behind an athlete, in the direction of the race or jump
a room or cabinet that keeps objects at a steady humidity

look.title: Men's Long Jump World Records
look.cite: World Athletics, men's long jump world record progression
look.prompt: Which jump made the biggest leap over the record before it? Where was it set?

check.q: How does thin air at high altitude affect sprints and jumps?
choices: It slows them down a lot.
It pushes back less, which can help them.
It has no effect at all.
check.why: Thin air creates less drag, which helps short, fast events like sprints and jumps.

check.q: Whose long jump record lasted from 1968 to 1991?
check.why: Beamon's 8.90 meters in Mexico City stood until Mike Powell's 8.95 in 1991.

check.q: What does a tailwind above 2.0 meters per second do to a sprint record?
choices: It stops the record from being ratified.
It marks the result with an A.
check.why: World Athletics does not ratify sprint or horizontal jump records with a tailwind over 2.0 meters per second.

lessons.title: The First Drug Tests
lessons.mainIdea: After a cyclist's death in 1967, the IOC formed a medical commission, and the first Olympic drug tests came in 1968.
reading: *Doping* means using banned drugs or methods to improve performance. On July 13, 1967, British cyclist Tom Simpson collapsed and died on Mont Ventoux during the Tour de France. Amphetamines, stimulant drugs, were found in his body. His death was widely reported and pushed sports leaders to act.

That same year, the International Olympic Committee formed a Medical Commission. It wrote a list of banned substances. At the 1968 Winter Games in Grenoble, France, and the Summer Games in Mexico City, Olympic athletes faced drug tests for the first time.

In Mexico City, Swedish modern pentathlete Hans-Gunnar Liljenwall became the first Olympian disqualified for a *banned substance*. His test showed alcohol, which was on the list at the time. His team lost its bronze medal. Tests for anabolic steroids, drugs that build muscle, were added in the mid-1970s. Each new test was a new rule about what counted in a record.

words.d: using banned drugs or methods to improve sports performance
a drug or other material that a sports body forbids athletes to use
drugs that help build muscle, banned in most sports
the IOC body formed in 1967 to set drug rules for the Olympics

look.title: A Rule Written After a Death
look.text: In July 1967, news spreads that a British cyclist has died on a mountain road during the Tour de France. Doctors find stimulant drugs in his body. Within months, Olympic leaders form a medical group. By the next Olympics, athletes must give samples for testing.
look.prompt: How does this case show a rule being made in response to a real event?

check.q: What does doping mean?
choices: using banned drugs or methods to improve performance
check.why: Doping is the use of banned drugs or methods to gain an edge.

check.q: When did Olympic athletes first face drug tests?
check.why: The first Olympic drug tests came at the 1968 Games in Grenoble and Mexico City.

check.q: Why was Hans-Gunnar Liljenwall disqualified in 1968?
choices: His test showed alcohol, a banned substance then.
check.why: Liljenwall tested positive for alcohol, which the IOC list banned at the time.

lessons.title: Seoul and a Secret Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Ben Johnson's 1988 disqualification and the exposure of East Germany's state doping program led toward a world anti-doping agency in 1999.
reading: On September 24, 1988, Canada's Ben Johnson won the Olympic 100 meters in Seoul in 9.79 seconds, a world record. Days later, officials announced that his sample showed stanozolol, an anabolic steroid. He lost the gold medal, which went to Carl Lewis of the United States. A Canadian government inquiry in 1989 heard Johnson admit he had used steroids.

East Germany had run a secret state doping program from the 1970s. After Germany reunited in 1990, files from the East German secret police and sports bodies were opened. They showed that thousands of athletes, many of them teenagers, were given drugs, often without being told what they were. In 2000, German courts convicted former top sports officials, including Manfred Ewald.

In 1998, police found banned drugs in a team car at the Tour de France. This scandal pushed sports leaders and governments to work together. The *World Anti-Doping Agency*, or WADA, was founded on November 10, 1999, in Lausanne, Switzerland. Its World Anti-Doping Code, in force from 2004, gave most sports one set of rules. A *sanction*, or penalty, now followed the same rules across many sports.

words.d: the body founded in 1999 to set shared drug rules across sports; called WADA
a penalty given for breaking a rule
an anabolic steroid; the drug found in Ben Johnson's 1988 sample

look.title: Files Opened After 1990
look.text: A researcher in the 1990s reads files from former East German offices. The pages list athletes, drug doses and dates. Some athletes were teenagers. Several later said they had been told the pills were vitamins. These files became evidence in court.
look.prompt: Why do written files make a stronger case than rumors about an athlete?

check.q: What happened to Ben Johnson's 1988 gold medal?
choices: It was split with Carl Lewis.
It was taken away after a positive steroid test.
It was given to an East German runner.
check.why: Johnson's sample showed stanozolol, so he lost the gold, which went to Carl Lewis.

check.q: How did the world learn details of East Germany's doping program?
choices: from files opened after Germany reunited in 1990
check.why: Government and secret police files were opened after reunification in 1990.

check.q: When and where was WADA founded?
check.why: The World Anti-Doping Agency was founded on November 10, 1999, in Lausanne, Switzerland.

lessons.title: Home Runs and a Report
lessons.mainIdea: Baseball's home run records of 1998 and 2001 came under doubt when a 2007 report documented steroid use in the sport.
reading: In 1998, Mark McGwire of the St. Louis Cardinals hit 70 home runs, and Sammy Sosa of the Chicago Cubs hit 66. Both passed Roger Maris's 61. Crowds and television ratings grew as the two chased the record. In 2001, Barry Bonds of the San Francisco Giants hit 73, the current single-season record.

At that time, Major League Baseball had no drug testing with penalties for its players. Survey testing began in 2003. Testing with penalties for steroids followed in 2004 and grew stricter in 2005. On December 13, 2007, former U.S. Senator George Mitchell released a report for the commissioner on steroid use in baseball. The *Mitchell Report* named dozens of players and said the problem had spread across the sport.

In 2010, McGwire publicly admitted he had used steroids, including in 1998. Major League Baseball did not remove the 1998 or 2001 records from its books. Instead, the argument moved to the Baseball Hall of Fame, where sportswriters vote on who is honored. The official record and the public's trust in it had come apart.

words.d: a 2007 report by George Mitchell on steroid use in Major League Baseball
drug tests used to measure how common drug use is, without penalties
a museum that honors chosen players, often by a vote of writers

check.q: Who hit 66 home runs for the Chicago Cubs in 1998?
check.why: Sammy Sosa of the Cubs hit 66 in 1998, while McGwire hit 70 for St. Louis.

check.q: What was the Mitchell Report?
choices: a 2007 report on steroid use in baseball
check.why: Former Senator George Mitchell released the report on December 13, 2007.

check.q: When did Major League Baseball begin penalties for steroid use?
check.why: Survey testing began in 2003, and testing with penalties followed in 2004.

lessons.title: Races Women Could Not Run
lessons.mainIdea: For decades women were barred from longer races, so their records in those events could not begin until the doors opened.
reading: Women first ran the 800 meters at the Olympics in 1928 in Amsterdam. Lina Radke of Germany won in a world record time. Some newspapers wrote false stories that the runners collapsed from exhaustion. Olympic and track leaders then dropped women's races longer than 200 meters. The women's 800 meters did not return to the Olympics until 1960.

Road races shut women out too. In 1966, Bobbi Gibb ran the Boston Marathon without an official number. In 1967, Kathrine Switzer entered as "K. V. Switzer" and wore number 261. A race official, Jock Semple, tried to pull her off the course, and photographers caught the scene. The Boston Marathon officially opened to women in 1972.

The first women's Olympic marathon was held in Los Angeles in 1984, and Joan Benoit of the United States won it. A record can only exist in an event people are allowed to enter. When the event is closed, there is no *record* to break, only an *exclusion*, a rule that keeps a group out. Many women's records are young because the doors opened late.

words.d: a rule or practice that keeps a group of people out
the best official mark ever made in an event
a running race of about 26.2 miles, or 42.195 kilometers

look.cite: International Olympic Committee, Olympic results records

check.q: Why was the women's 800 meters dropped after 1928?
choices: Leaders acted on false reports that runners collapsed.
check.why: False newspaper stories about exhaustion led leaders to drop women's races over 200 meters until 1960.

check.q: What does exclusion mean?
choices: a rule or practice that keeps a group out
a race run at high altitude
check.why: Exclusion means keeping a group out, as long races did to women for decades.

check.q: When did the Boston Marathon officially open to women?
check.why: Women ran without numbers or under initials before, but Boston officially admitted them in 1972.

lessons.title: The Negro Leagues Enter the Book
lessons.mainIdea: In 2020, Major League Baseball recognized seven Negro Leagues as major leagues, and in 2024 their statistics joined its records.
reading: In February 1920, Rube Foster, owner of the Chicago American Giants, led a meeting in Kansas City that founded the Negro National League. Black players built their own leagues because the major leagues kept them out under an unwritten *color line*. That line held until Jackie Robinson played for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947.

Josh Gibson, a catcher for teams including the Homestead Grays, was one of the most famous Negro League players. He never had the chance to play in the major leagues. He died in January 1947, months before Robinson's first game. Stories that Gibson hit about 800 home runs are legends passed down by fans and players. No complete game records prove that number.

On December 16, 2020, Major League Baseball announced that seven Negro Leagues from 1920 to 1948 would count as major leagues. In May 2024, their *statistics* joined MLB's official records. Researchers built those numbers from box scores in Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier. Gibson's .372 career batting average became the highest in major league records, passing Ty Cobb.

words.d: the unwritten rule that kept Black players out of white professional leagues
numbers collected and counted to describe what happened
a league of Black professional baseball teams founded in 1920

look.title: Legend and Record Side by Side
look.text: A fan says Josh Gibson hit about 800 home runs. The official records, built from surviving box scores, list far fewer, because many games were never written down or the papers were lost. Both the legend and the record try to describe the same great hitter.
look.prompt: Why do historians keep the legend and the documented record separate?

check.q: Who led the 1920 meeting that founded the Negro National League?
check.why: Rube Foster of the Chicago American Giants led the Kansas City meeting in February 1920.

check.q: What did MLB announce on December 16, 2020?
choices: It would ban Negro League records.
It would move the Hall of Fame.
Seven Negro Leagues from 1920 to 1948 would count as major leagues.
check.why: MLB recognized seven Negro Leagues as major leagues and added their statistics in 2024.

check.q: Where did researchers find many Negro League numbers?
choices: box scores in Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender
check.why: Researchers rebuilt the statistics from box scores printed in Black newspapers.

lessons.title: Doubt Needs Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Questioning a record is fair when there is a specific reason, such as a faulty gauge, a failed test or documents.
reading: On July 16, 1988, at the U.S. Olympic Trials in Indianapolis, Florence Griffith Joyner ran the women's 100 meters in 10.49 seconds. The official wind gauge read 0.0 meters per second. Other gauges nearby showed strong winds at about the same time. Some experts argued the gauge was faulty. The mark was ratified anyway and still stands as the world record.

Doubt about that race rests on a specific piece of *evidence*: the wind readings. That is different from doubt based only on how amazing a time looks. Some women's track records from the 1980s have stood for decades, and people argue about them. The women's 800 meters record, 1:53.28, was set in 1983 and is the oldest individual world record in track and field.

In 2017, European Athletics proposed resetting world records set before 2005, the year stored drug samples began to be kept for ten years for retesting. Athletes who had never broken a rule protested that they would lose their records unfairly. The idea was not adopted. The debate showed a key idea in record keeping: *suspicion* alone is not proof, and a fair challenge names its reason.

words.d: facts or records that show whether something is true
a feeling that something may be wrong, without proof
a device that measures wind speed during a race or jump

look.title: Three Kinds of Doubt
look.text: Claim 1: "That time is too fast to be real." Claim 2: "The wind gauge read zero while gauges nearby read high winds." Claim 3: "Opened government files list this athlete's drug doses." All three question a record. Only some point to something a judge could check.
look.prompt: Rank the three claims from weakest to strongest evidence, and explain your ranking.

check.q: What evidence raised doubts about the 10.49 time in 1988?

check.why: The official gauge read 0.0 while other gauges showed strong wind, so experts questioned it.

check.q: What is the difference between suspicion and evidence?
choices: Evidence is a fact that can be checked; suspicion is a feeling without proof.
check.why: Suspicion is a feeling; evidence is a fact or record that shows whether something is true.

choices: It was adopted only for swimming.
It became law in the United States.
check.why: Athletes objected that clean records would be lost unfairly, and the idea was not adopted.

review.q: Which change led track and field to start a new men's javelin record list in 1986?
review.why: The center of gravity was moved forward, so the new javelin was treated as a different tool.

review.q: What did the 1961 Maris argument and the 2008 swimsuit argument share?
choices: Both asked whether marks made under different conditions could be compared.
review.why: One was about a longer schedule and the other about new suits; both were arguments about context.

review.q: Which record was set at high altitude?
review.why: Beamon jumped in Mexico City in 1968, about 2,240 meters above sea level.
Olympic tests began in 1968; Johnson was disqualified in 1988, WADA formed in 1999 and the Mitchell Report came in 2007.

review.q: Why can't old women's marathon records exist from the 1950s Olympics?
choices: Women were not allowed to run an Olympic marathon until 1984.
The races were at high altitude.
review.why: The first women's Olympic marathon was held in 1984, so no earlier Olympic record could exist.

review.q: Why did Josh Gibson's career average enter MLB records in 2024?
choices: He played in the major leagues after 1947.
MLB recognized the Negro Leagues and added their statistics.
SABR voted him into the Hall of Fame.
review.why: After MLB recognized seven Negro Leagues in 2020, their statistics joined its records in 2024.

review.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to doubt a record?
choices: The athlete is from another country.
A wind gauge reading disagrees with nearby gauges.
review.why: A conflicting gauge reading is specific evidence that can be checked.

review.q: What does an official scorer decide?
choices: whether a play counts as a hit or an error
review.why: The official scorer rules on hits, errors and other game numbers under the Official Baseball Rules.
